title: Hawaiʻi CKMR Workshop 2026
text:
Welcome
Welcome to the Hawaiʻi CKMR Workshop 2026, taught by Mark Bravington and Eric Anderson.
This is our course web page: a clearinghouse for links to the slides, exercises, code, data, and other materials you will need. We will update it as the workshop goes along. Many of the materials will be hosted on the instructors’ GitHub pages or in their GitHub repositories; we will introduce them and add links here as we use them.

title: Hawaiʻi CKMR Workshop 2026
text:
Prepare your laptop
Please prepare R and the packages for both instructors’ hands-on exercises before the workshop. R 4.6.x is the recommended starting point, with pre-built packages for a broad range of supported Mac and Windows systems. Mark’s packages also have builds for other R versions, including R 4.5.x on Mac and Windows; see his setup page for the platform/version options.
Installation commands for required packages can be run in the R console. See the following links for explicit commands.

Install packages for Mark’s hands-on exercises
Install packages and prepare for Eric’s hands-on exercises

title: Hawaiʻi CKMR Workshop 2026
text:
Do some pre-workshop reading
This course is intended to provide a “cold start,” meaning we build up CKMR concepts from their foundations without requiring prior knowledge. Nonetheless, if you wish to read up on CKMR before the workshop, or during your flight to Hawaiʻi, we recommend two readings, each with a different flavor.

If you enjoy mathematical statistics and notation, the fundamentals of CKMR are laid out in those terms in Bravington, Skaug, and Anderson (2016). Close-kin mark-recapture. Statistical Science 31:259-274.
For a more accessible introduction to CKMR, we recommend Bravington and Carroll (2023). The practical magic of close-kin mark-recapture. CSIRO Publishing (download PDF). To download it, accept Mark’s emailed invitation to his private GitHub repository and sign in with the GitHub account associated with that invitation.

Essential reading: Please read Mark’s 2026 R cribsheet (PDF). Reading this ahead of time can help immensely. Mark has developed an R ecosystem of packages and functions, and he relies on R environments for computational efficiency and syntactic brevity. This may be unfamiliar to some R users. His cribsheet provides an essential introduction.

title: Hawaiʻi CKMR Workshop 2026
text:
BYOS — Bring your own species
The workshop agenda includes worked examples for a series of different species that illustrate real-life scenarios. In addition, the extended nature of the course is intended to provide participants with a chance to apply principles of CKMR design to their own species of interest. For such design, it is not necessary to know everything, but we provide brief BYOS guidelines for key pieces of information you’ll want to be armed with.

title: Hawaiʻi CKMR Workshop 2026
text:
Workshop agenda
The current agenda is below. Exactly what happens when is flexible: we will adjust to the pace of the workshop. The three additional workshop days after the formal course offer a chance to explore topics more deeply and to work on specific fisheries/species of interest.
Download the original agenda (PDF)

Monday, November 9

Introduction: principles, scope, and workshop overview
Parent-offspring pairs (POPs): simple marine mammal example and model
Gotchas #1: because nothing is ever that simple…

Gotchas #2: HSPs are a rich source of gotchas
And so to fish: basic CKMR-driven fish model

title: Hawaiʻi CKMR Workshop 2026
text:
Course materials
Mark’s course repository is the starting point for his workshop materials. The repository will be private during the course. Mark has invited participants by email; please accept your invitation and sign in to GitHub with the account associated with it to access the materials. We will introduce the materials separately during the course; you do not need repository access to install Mark’s packages.
Links to slides, exercises, and other resources will be added as the workshop progresses.

title: Mark’s setup
text:
Choose an R version
Install these packages before the 2026 workshop if you plan to run Mark’s hands-on exercises on your laptop. These instructions cover package dependencies; the scripts, datasets, and other course materials will get their own introduction.
Running code is optional for Mark’s part of the course: you are welcome to participate by following the concepts without running the examples yourself.
You do not need access to Mark’s course GitHub repository for this setup: his packages are distributed through R-universe.
Download Mark’s 2026 R cribsheet (PDF) for the full notes. For installation, copy the commands from this web page: copying code from the PDF can introduce extra spaces, line breaks, and other characters that need cleaning up before R can run it.
R 4.6.x is our recommended starting point, but it is not a strict requirement for Mark’s exercises. If you already use R 4.5.x on Mac or Windows, try the installation and checks below before upgrading.
Mark expects R 4.5.x to work, but has not tested it recently. The build information below is supplementary guidance: available package builds do not establish that the course examples have been tested with every listed R version.
Mark’s R-universe build matrix currently shows the following builds for his packages (checked October 29, 2026):
R 4.7 builds are useful if you already use development R; there is no need to switch to a development version for this course.
Use the package-loading checks below to confirm your own installation, including the CRAN dependencies. lyxport is not needed for this course.

title: Mark’s setup
text:
Install the packages
Start a fresh R session. Add Mark’s R-universe while preserving your existing repositories and including CRAN as a fallback:
options(repos = unique(c(
  "https://markbravington.r-universe.dev",
  getOption("repos"),
  "https://cloud.r-project.org"
)))
Install the CRAN packages first:
install.packages(c("doParallel", "RTMB"))
If that succeeds, install Mark’s package collection. mvbjoblot brings in all the other packages needed for his exercises:
install.packages("mvbjoblot")
Use Mark’s R-universe distributions for his packages. Older versions on CRAN may be out of date; downloading his individual package repositories from GitHub is unnecessary.






NoteRepository settings last for this R session



If you restart R before installing or reinstalling Mark’s packages, run the options(repos = ...) block again.

title: Mark’s setup
text:
Check your installation
Try loading the packages with the most dependencies:
library(offartmb)
library(despack)
If both load without errors, your package setup is ready.

title: Mark’s setup
text:
If installation fails
An installation error does not necessarily prevent you from participating. Save the error message so we can see which package failed.






TipTroubleshooting and the minimum package set





The packages Matrix, Rcpp, and TMB can have version conflicts. If the error points to these packages, try reinstalling them in that order. Run the repository-settings block above first if you have restarted R.
install.packages("Matrix")
install.packages("Rcpp")
install.packages("TMB")
Then retry the failed installation. If an error specifically requires installing Rcpp or TMB from source, you will need the appropriate build tools.
The full set of non-default CRAN dependencies listed in the original cribsheet is doParallel, foreach, iterators, Rcpp, RcppEigen, RTMB, and TMB; Matrix can also be involved in version conflicts.
For most exercises, the essential packages are mvbutils, atease, and offarray. Loading offarray also loads the other two:
library(offarray)
The design exercises additionally need microscoping and despack:
library(microscoping)
library(despack)
deconvodisc is an optional dependency used in a couple of examples; it is not part of the installation check above. offartmb supports fitting examples with RTMB, an optional alternative to the native R fits. If TMB or RTMB will not install, you can still follow much of the course using the native R examples.



Adapted from the installation section of Mark Bravington’s 2026 R cribsheet.

title: Eric’s setup
text:
Build tools
For Eric’s exercises, use R 4.6.x or R 4.5.x. Install CKMRsim from GitHub, and install the packages needed for CKMRshiny. RStudio Desktop is helpful but optional.
CKMRsim contains compiled code and installs from source when downloaded from GitHub. If you don’t already have them, set up the build tools for your operating system.

title: Eric’s setup
text:
Windows
Install the toolchain recommended for your R version on the official Rtools page. R 4.6 uses Rtools45; the toolchain number does not always match the R version. Use the default installer settings, then restart RStudio (or R) before continuing.


macOS
Install Apple’s Command Line Tools for Xcode. Run the following in Terminal, rather than the R console, and follow the installation prompts:
xcode-select --install
If the tools are already installed, macOS will tell you. CKMRsim uses C/C++ through Rcpp.


Linux
Install the C/C++ compiler, make, and R development files supplied by your distribution. On Debian/Ubuntu, these are generally provided by build-essential and r-base-dev. Some tidyverse dependencies may also need system libraries; use the installation error messages to identify any missing development packages.

title: Eric’s setup
text:
Install R packages
Run these commands in the R console:
install.packages(
  c("remotes", "tidyverse", "shiny"),
  repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
)

remotes::install_github("eriqande/CKMRsim", build_vignettes = FALSE)
CKMRsim’s required R dependencies are installed automatically. Building its vignettes is unnecessary for this setup.

title: Eric’s setup
text:
Check the packages
The following should run without errors:
library(CKMRsim)
library(tidyverse)
library(shiny)
library(ggplot2)
library(tibble)

title: Eric’s setup
text:
Download and run CKMRshiny
CKMRshiny is a repository that contains a couple of Shiny applications and a few R Markdown documents, rather than an R package. You do not install it with install_github().
The best way to get it is to clone it from GitHub. Either:

Get it with git clone on the command line:

git clone https://github.com/eriqande/CKMRshiny.git
Or use RStudio to clone it as a new project.
After that:

Open the CKMRshiny RStudio project (or set your working directory to that folder). The folder should contain app.R and the R subfolder.
Run the app from Rstudio by opening app.R and choosing “Run App”

Or
run the app from the R console:
shiny::runApp()
Alternatively, give runApp() the path to the extracted folder:
shiny::runApp("path/to/CKMRshiny-main")
Replace the example path with the actual folder on your computer. The app should open with tabs for equal reproduction, randomly unequal reproduction, and size-based reproduction. Run a small trial to check that plots appear. Stop the app with RStudio’s Stop button or by pressing Esc in the R console.

title: Eric’s setup
text:
If you get stuck
Restart R and try loading the packages again. For a CKMRsim installation failure, first check that the compiler tools are installed and read the first error in the installation output. Save that error message and your R version (R.version.string) so we can help diagnose the problem.

title: BYOS guidelines
text:
Simple designs
Our group probably won’t be able to do 30 separate case studies of CKMR design, but we are looking forward to working together on the steps of CKMR design for some different species of interest.
For preliminary simple designs (along the lines of Mark’s microscoping package) the data needs are fairly minimal: keeping to the basics is fine here.
For all species you’ll want to have a handle on:

title: BYOS guidelines
text:
A ballpark estimate of population size
Qualitative features of the species’ biology
Any information available on population structure and connectivity
What sort of sampling can be done for the species and the sampling selectivity that might affect those samples
For fish-like species, typical outputs from a recent assessment:

Numbers at age
Weight at age
Maturity schedule

title: BYOS guidelines
text:
More complex designs
Moving beyond the simple microscoping types of design, be prepared to answer more questions:

What is the relationship between fecundity and size?
Are catch-at-age data/estimates available?
How many samples can I age?

title: BYOS guidelines
text:
Genotype data
Some of you might have genotype data from species of interest. Whether you have just enough to estimate allele frequencies or an entire collection of samples, bring those data along and we can explore them with CKMRsim or kinference.
